newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hitachi yields to Toshiba in earnings race.
newsitem.headline: Hitachi yields to Toshiba in earnings race.

text.p: Hitachi Ltd, long the king of Japan's integrated electronics firms, was toppled from the top post in profits last year as a protracted freefall in memory chip prices threw a wrench into its profit engine.

Hitachi, which sells everything from nuclear power plants to microchips, said on Thursday that its parent current profit slid 34.5 percent to 84.32 billion yen ($726 million) in the year ended on March 31.
"Sluggish chip prices dragged down the overall profit, although the heavy machinery sector managed to post a small profit," Hitachi executive managing director Yoshiki Yagi told a news conference.

Hitachi for the first time in more than 50 years ceded the top post in parent profits to archrival Toshiba Corp, which earlier this week announced a parent current profit of 96.80 billion yen ($834 million) for the year.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses from securities investments and other non-operating activities.

While Japan's big comprehensive electronics makers -- Hitachi, Toshiba and Mitsubishi Electric Corp -- all suffered from weak chip prices, sluggish consumer electronics business and declining profit in heavy machinery, Toshiba managed to cushion the triple blow with booming personal computer sales.
Hitachi, on the other hand, has been slow to develop its PC business, while its strength lies in large mainframe computers and network systems.
"Hitachi tends to benefit from Japan's boom in communications infrastructure," said Mami Indo, analyst at Daiwa Research Institute.
"But profit growth in this field could be slower than that of its rivals, because Hitachi's clients are mostly financial institutions, major casualties of Japan's bad-loan crisis," she said.

Yagi said Hitachi expects its parent current profit to jump 30 percent to 110 billion yen ($948 million) in fiscal 1997/98, citing increasing profits from telecommunications equipment and computer displays.

He added, however, that operating profit from heavy machinery and power plants, Hitachi's single biggest source of income, would decrease by more than 10 percent in 1997/98 due to a squeeze in public works spending and the slow recovery of the domestic economy.
At the same time, Hitachi expects a gain of more than 10 percent during the year in profits from the information sector, which includes telecommunications equipment, computers and chips.
